a-world-awakened:
Welcome. I'm so glad you're here. Before we take our first step, let's take a moment to breathe, to quiet the noise of the day, and to open our hearts. You are about to walk through the story of the Bible, from the very first words to the very last, as one continuous story. Not a collection of random passages, but one great story of God and the people he loves.

Here is how our journey will unfold. We will travel through twelve periods. We begin right here, in the Beginnings, where God creates the world and everything in it, and where humanity first turns away from him. Then we follow a family. God calls Abraham, and through Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, he promises to bless the whole world. That family ends up in Egypt, enslaved, and God sets them free in the Exodus and makes a covenant with them at Sinai. They wander in the desert, where they are tested and formed, and then they enter the Promised Land. Soon the people ask for a king, and we meet Saul, David, and Solomon. After Solomon, the kingdom splits in two, and the prophets rise up, calling God's people back to him. Then comes exile, when Jerusalem falls and the people are carried off to Babylon. Yet God brings them home, and they rebuild. In a time of great pressure, the Maccabees stand firm in faith. And then, at the center of everything, comes Jesus: his life, his death, and his resurrection. The story does not end there. The Church is born, the gospel travels to the ends of the earth, and the story points us to its final chapter, when God makes all things new.

When you see it all together, something wonderful appears. The Bible is not a rulebook. It is a family story, and you are invited into it. So as you listen, don't rush. Let these stories speak to you. Ask God to meet you in them. And if a story stirs something in you, pause and stay there for a while.

Now, let's begin where everything begins. Before there were mountains, or oceans, or stars, there was God. And God spoke. In this first period, we will hear about creation, about a garden, about a choice that changed everything, and about a promise of hope that God whispered even in the darkest moment. As you listen, hold onto one question: what kind of God makes a world like this, and then refuses to give up on the people in it? Let's find out together.
a-promise-takes-root:
Welcome back. Take a breath, and let's catch up on where we are. In the Beginnings, God made a good world, and humanity broke it. We saw Adam and Eve leave the garden, Cain's jealousy, the flood, and a tower at Babel that ended with people scattered and their voices confused. If the story had ended there, it would be a sad one. But here is where everything turns.

God does not give up on the whole world. Instead, he starts small. He calls one man, Abraham, and one woman, Sarah, who are old, childless, and far from home, and he makes a promise: through your family, I will bless every family on earth. Everything we read from here to the end of the Bible grows out of that one promise.

This family is not a perfect one, and I think you will be glad of that. There is laughter and doubt, favoritism and deception, and jealousy so deep that brothers sell their own brother. And yet, again and again, God keeps showing up in the middle of the mess. He is not waiting for them to be impressive. He is simply faithful.

Keep your eyes open for two moments that reach far beyond their own time. On a mountain, a father is asked to give up the son he loves, and God provides a lamb instead. Remember that picture, because one day another Father will give his own Son. And later you will meet Joseph, betrayed by his own brothers, sold, forgotten in prison, and then lifted up to save the very people who wronged him. Does that remind you of anyone?

A quiet challenge before we begin. Abraham was asked to leave everything familiar with no map, only a promise. Is there somewhere in your own life where God is inviting you to trust him a little more than you can see? Hold that question gently as we listen.
freedom-and-belonging:
Welcome back. Let's pause for a moment and remember where we are. In the Beginnings, God made a good world, and humanity turned away, yet God never stopped pursuing us. Then he called Abraham and promised that through his family, the whole world would be blessed. We watched that promise pass from Abraham to Isaac, to Jacob, and to Joseph, whose life took his family down into Egypt to survive a famine. And that's where we pick up today.

But time has passed, and the story has taken a painful turn. The family that came as guests has grown into a great nation, and Egypt now sees them as a threat. The people who once were honored are now slaves. Can you imagine it? Generations of silence. Generations of crying out, with no answer in sight. If you have ever prayed for something for a very long time and wondered whether God was listening, you will understand them better than you think.

But God was listening. This period tells us that he hears the cry of the oppressed, he knows their names, and he comes down to rescue them. You will meet Moses, a shepherd who never asked for this job. You will hear the voice from a burning bush. You will witness the night of the Passover, when a lamb is slain and its blood marks the doors of God's people, and you will stand at the edge of the sea as it parts. Listen closely to the Passover. Centuries later, John the Baptist will point at a man and say, behold, the Lamb of God. This night is a shadow, and Jesus is the light that casts it.

But notice something else. God doesn't just free his people and leave them there. At Mount Sinai he says, I brought you out so that you could belong to me. Freedom, in the Bible, is never just freedom from something. It is freedom for something. It is freedom to belong, to be loved, to love back. And yes, we will also see how quickly the people forget, with the golden calf, and how patiently God keeps his covenant anyway.

So as you listen, ask yourself an honest question. What is the Egypt in my own life, the thing that holds me, that I've stopped believing I could escape? And what might it look like to let God lead me out? Let's walk out of Egypt together.
a-kingdom-under-question:
Welcome back, friend. Let's remember the last stretch of road. God heard the cry of his people in Egypt, brought them through the sea, and bound himself to them in a covenant at Sinai. They were free. And now? You might expect the next scene to be a grand arrival in a beautiful land. Instead, the next scene is a desert.

This is a period about the in-between. The people are no longer slaves, but they have not yet reached the promise. They are hungry, thirsty, and tired, and in their discomfort a surprising thing happens. They start to remember Egypt as if it were not so bad. Have you ever done that? Preferred a familiar hardship over an uncertain freedom?

But watch what God does in the desert. When they are hungry, he sends bread from heaven each morning, just enough for the day. When they are thirsty, water pours out of a rock. When they are afraid, and they will be, because ten of the twelve spies come back full of fear, he is patient, even as he allows the consequences of their choices to unfold. And when they are bitten by serpents, he gives them something to look at, a bronze serpent lifted up on a pole, and everyone who looks is healed. Hold on to that image. Jesus himself will say, as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up. And the bread from heaven? Jesus will call himself that too.

The desert is not only a punishment. It is a school. It is where God forms a people who learn to depend on him one day at a time. And this period ends with Moses, who has led them faithfully for forty years, standing on a mountain and looking at a land he will not enter.

So if you are in a wilderness season right now, a season of waiting, of dryness, of not yet, take heart. This part of the story was written for you. Let's walk into the desert together.
voices-for-the-road-home:
Welcome back. Moses has died, and the whole nation stands at the edge of the Jordan River with the Promised Land finally in view. After all those years in the desert, can you feel the moment? Now the question is who will lead them in, and the answer is a man named Joshua. Here is something wonderful. Joshua's name in Hebrew is Yeshua, which is the same name we translate as Jesus. A Joshua leads God's people into the land, and a greater Joshua will one day lead us into something far greater. Keep that in the back of your mind.

In this period, we cross the river on dry ground, watch the walls of Jericho fall, and hear Joshua's famous farewell: choose today whom you will serve. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. That is one of the most beautiful lines in all of Scripture.

But then the story gets honest. After Joshua's generation passes, the people drift, and we enter the time of the judges, a cycle that repeats again and again. The people forget God, trouble comes, they cry out, God raises up a rescuer, and peace returns, until they forget again. It might sound familiar. We are not so different, are we? Yet notice the quiet mercy in it. Every time they cry out, God answers.

And then, in the middle of that rough era, a small and tender story appears, the story of Ruth. A foreigner, a widow, with nothing to her name, chooses to stay loyal to her mother in law and to the God of Israel. And God weaves her into the family line of King David, and ultimately of Jesus. Never think your small acts of faithfulness go unnoticed.

We finish with a boy named Samuel, lying down in the temple at night, hearing a voice call his name. As you listen, ask yourself, what would it sound like if I said, speak, Lord, your servant is listening? Let's begin.
good-news-in-a-small-town:
Welcome back. Last time, we watched the people of Israel settle in the land, and we heard a young Samuel say, speak, Lord, your servant is listening. But the people have a problem. They look around at the neighboring nations, with their kings and armies, and they say, give us a king too. God is their king, but they want what everyone else has. And so begins a very dramatic chapter.

First comes Saul, tall and impressive, but whose heart does not stay true. Then, out in the fields with the sheep, God chooses someone no one expected. A shepherd boy, the youngest of his family, the one even his father forgot to call in. Man looks at the outward appearance, but God looks at the heart. You will see him face a giant with nothing but a sling, and you will see him become king, bring the ark to Jerusalem, and dance for joy before the Lord.

Now, listen carefully to one moment, because it echoes through everything that follows. David wants to build God a house, and God says, no, I will build you a house. A royal line, a kingdom that will last forever. Every Israelite after that would look for a son of David who would reign without end. And when the angel speaks to Mary many centuries later, those very promises come back. That is why the Gospels begin by calling Jesus the son of David.

Then we meet Solomon, who asks God not for riches or a long life, but for wisdom. What a prayer. He builds the temple, and his dedication prayer is breathtaking. And yet, sadly, even wise Solomon drifts, and his heart becomes divided.

There is a lesson hiding here. Gifts and greatness do not protect us. Faithfulness does. So as you listen, take a moment to ask yourself, if God offered me anything, what would I ask for? Let's find out what these kings can teach us.
love-given-to-the-end:
Welcome back. Take a breath, because this period is a long and sometimes heavy one, and I want you to walk through it with open eyes and an open heart. Let's recall where we left off. David and Solomon built a great kingdom and a glorious temple, but Solomon's heart wandered, and God said the kingdom would be torn. That is where we begin.

The kingdom splits in two, Israel in the north and Judah in the south. King after king rises and falls, and most of them lead the people further from God. It can feel like watching a slow tragedy. But here is what I want you to notice. God does not stay silent. He sends prophets. Elijah stands alone on Mount Carmel and challenges a whole nation to stop limping between two opinions. Amos calls for justice to roll down like a river. And Hosea, in one of the most tender passages in the Bible, reveals the heart of God: when Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son. It is God speaking like a heartbroken parent who taught a child to walk, and who was turned away. Centuries later, Matthew will hear those words and see Jesus.

Yet judgment does come. The northern kingdom falls to Assyria. The south holds on a little longer, and there are bright spots, Hezekiah who prays when the enemy surrounds Jerusalem, and Josiah who rediscovers the law and renews the covenant. But Jeremiah warns that hearts must change, not only buildings, and in the end Jerusalem falls to Babylon.

If you feel sadness as you listen, that's okay. Sit with it. And look for the thread of mercy that runs through every page. God never stops sending voices, never stops calling his people home. Is there a voice that God has been sending you that you have been slow to hear? Let's listen.
morning-beyond-the-stone:
Welcome back. The last period ended with the unthinkable. Jerusalem is in ruins, the temple is burned, and the people have been marched hundreds of miles away to Babylon. Everything they thought was permanent is gone. How do you worship God when your temple is rubble? How do you sing when you are far from home?

This period is for anyone who has ever lost something they thought they could not lose. It begins with a family in Assyria, Tobit and Sarah, ordinary people in a foreign land, trying to live faithfully, praying out of deep pain, and discovering that God has been working behind the scenes in ways they could not see. Then comes Daniel, a young man in the palace of Babylon who decides, quietly, that he will not let the empire shape his heart. And when his faithfulness costs him, he finds himself in a den of lions, and he finds that he is not alone.

Then comes a psalm you may never forget: by the rivers of Babylon, we sat down and wept. It does not hide the grief. God does not ask us to pretend. And then the prophet Ezekiel is taken to a valley full of dry bones, and God asks him a question I want you to carry with you. Can these bones live? The answer will take your breath away. God says he will open the graves and breathe his Spirit into his people, and they will live. Hold on to that vision. It is a promise of resurrection long before the first Easter.

Here is my invitation. Most of us, at some point, feel like exiles, people living in a place that does not quite feel like home. The question is how we live there. Do we lose heart, or do we, like Daniel, like Tobit, stay faithful right where we are? Let's listen together, and let God breathe on whatever feels dry in us.
a-welcome-without-borders:
Welcome back. We have just walked through the long night of exile, and now something wonderful happens. A new king rises in Persia, and he opens the door. Go home, he says. Rebuild. Can you imagine the joy of that first step out of captivity? God had promised it through the prophets, and now we see him keep his word.

This period is about rebuilding, and it is honest about how hard rebuilding is. The exiles return, lay the foundation of the temple, and the air fills with shouts of joy and with the weeping of the elders who remember the old temple. Opposition comes, the work stops, and the prophet Haggai has to stir them up again, because it is so easy to get busy with our own houses while God's house sits unfinished. Eventually, the temple stands again.

Along the way, we meet a remarkable young woman named Esther, far from Jerusalem, who risks everything for her people. Who knows, her cousin tells her, whether you were placed here for a time like this. Perhaps you will wonder what moments in your own life God has placed you for.

Then Ezra, a scribe devoted to God's law, and Nehemiah, a cupbearer with a burden for his broken city, help rebuild the walls in just fifty two days. And then comes my favorite scene. The people gather in the square, Ezra opens the book of the law, and they weep as they hear it. But Nehemiah tells them, do not grieve, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.

The period ends with a quiet promise from Malachi, that God will send a messenger to prepare the way. Remember that. Centuries later, John the Baptist will fulfill it.

So here is something to take with you. Whatever feels broken, a relationship, a habit, a season of life, God is a rebuilder. What is one stone you could lay today? Let's go home together.
the-maccabean-resistance:
Welcome back. We have just closed the Hebrew prophets with Malachi's promise that a messenger is coming. But the messenger does not come right away. Instead, there are hundreds of years of waiting. Empires rise and fall, and the Jewish people find themselves under Greek rule, in a world where their faith and their way of life are no longer the norm. Many are tempted to blend in.

This short period is about what happens when faith is tested under pressure. A powerful king named Antiochus tries to force the people to abandon their covenant, to eat what the law forbids, to offer sacrifices to false gods, and to give up the Scriptures. Some give in. But others do not. An elderly priest named Mattathias says, even if all the nations obey the king, I and my sons will walk in the covenant of our ancestors. And a revolt begins.

You will also hear one of the most moving stories in the Bible, of a mother and her seven sons, each facing death rather than betray God. And listen to what they believe. They speak, with remarkable confidence, about God raising them up. Hope in the resurrection shines brighter here than ever before, preparing the way for the gospel.

And finally, the temple that had been defiled is cleansed and rededicated, a celebration still remembered today as Hanukkah. In fact, the Gospel of John tells us that Jesus himself walked in the temple during that feast.

I'll leave you with a question. What are the things I will not compromise, not for convenience, not for comfort, not even for safety? And do I trust that God is faithful to those who are faithful to him, even beyond death? Let's listen.
learning-to-be-one-body:
Welcome back, and welcome to the heart of the entire journey. Everything we have walked through so far has been leading to this. The promise to Abraham, the freedom from Egypt, the throne of David, the cries of the prophets, the long years of waiting. Now, in a small town, in a young woman's yes, the Word becomes flesh.

Let me recap quickly, because it matters. A world was made good and then broken. A family was chosen to carry a promise. A people was freed and given a covenant. They were formed in the desert, settled in a land, ruled by kings, scattered by exile, brought home, and tested by persecution. And through it all, God kept pointing ahead to someone who was coming.

In this period, we follow Jesus through the Gospel of Luke. We will stand at Mary's side at the Annunciation, kneel at the manger, and hear Jesus read from the scroll in Nazareth, good news to the poor. We will watch him call fishermen, heal a paralyzed man, and shine with glory on the mountain. We will hear one of his greatest parables, of a father who runs to welcome a lost son, and I hope you will hear yourself in it. And then we will walk with him into Jerusalem.

I want to be honest with you. The path from here becomes difficult. We will sit at a table with him on the last night, pray with him in the garden, and stand at the foot of the cross. Take your time with those stories. Don't hurry. Let them be what they are.

But hold on, because the story does not end at the cross. On the third day, an empty tomb, and then a stranger on the road to Emmaus whose words set hearts burning. I encourage you to listen to these stories not only as history, but as an encounter. Jesus is not a character stuck in the past. He is alive, and he meets people on the road, just like you and me. Let's walk with him.
the-story-in-our-hands:
Welcome back. This is the final period of our journey, and what a way to finish. Let's remember where we left off. Jesus has died and risen, he has appeared to his friends, and he has ascended, with a promise: you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses. Now the disciples, a small and frightened group, wait in an upper room. Nobody knows what happens next.

And then comes Pentecost. Wind, fire, and a sound that fills the house. Peter, the same Peter who denied Jesus, stands up and preaches boldly, and thousands come to believe. And what do those first believers do? They share their meals, their belongings, and their prayers. It is worth pausing on that picture. This is what the Church was meant to look like, a family.

From there, the story pushes outward. Stephen is stoned, yet he forgives, and a young man named Saul watches. Then a bright light on the road to Damascus, and the persecutor becomes Paul, the great missionary. Peter learns that the gospel is for everyone, Jew and Gentile alike. The apostles meet in Jerusalem to decide how to welcome the nations. Paul crosses seas and cities, speaks to philosophers in Athens, and finally arrives in Rome, proclaiming the kingdom of God boldly and without hindrance.

Notice how this story ends. Not with a tidy conclusion, but with the message still moving. The last pages of the Bible look ahead to the day God makes all things new, and until then, we live in between, as witnesses. The book of Acts is still being written, and you are part of it.

So let me leave you with a challenge. Who in your life needs to hear about the hope you have received? And what small step of courage might the Spirit be inviting you to take this week? You have walked from creation all the way to the early Church. The story of Scripture is not behind you. It is inside you. Let's finish this journey together.
